provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation:
In the original task, every single-colour object moves 'down' by a number of cells equal to its own cell count. Any cells that go past the grid edge are dropped. The background is colour 7.

Under D4, a row reversal does not change a vertical direction vector. Each clockwise rotation maps a direction (dr, dc) to (dc, -dr). So 'down' becomes left for k=1, up for k=2 and right for k=3. The factory bakes this visible direction vector (DR, DC) into the emitted program as constants, and it sets the background constant to palette[7].

The emitted program starts from a background canvas. It finds connected components for each non-background colour, using 8-connectivity so it is robust if sprites are only diagonally connected. It then stamps each component's cells shifted by size*(DR, DC) directly in visible coordinates, clipping anything that falls outside the grid. Demonstrations are not needed.
draft_notes.limitations: Assumes that, as in the generator, objects of different colours never touch each other (they are separated by a 1-cell margin). Assumes that shifted objects never collide; the generator guarantees this because objects occupy disjoint column ranges along the motion axis. If a collision did occur, the colour processed later (in sorted colour order) would win, which is not a rule of the puzzle. Also assumes that within one colour, distinct objects are not diagonally adjacent; the generator uses one object per colour. The background is fixed to palette[7] rather than inferred. No constructor defects were found, and the fixtures are consistent with the uniform rule.
